transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because of the ongoing situation at my apartment. For months now, the property manager and certain people in the building have been... well, they're trying to pressure me out. 

It started with misdelivered mail. Which is funny, because the postal service used to be the gold standard of efficiency. When I was getting my master's degree, I actually did a whole statistical breakdown on mail sorting logistics for a project. We had to use punch cards back then, if you can believe it. Took hours just to run a simple regression. 

But anyway, now? At my building? It's all deliberate. They use the mail, and they time these noises in the walls just perfectly, along with these little comments from the neighbors when I walk by. They try to hand me paperwork and give me these long-winded explanations to explain it all away, but no amount of their paperwork changes the pattern I can clearly see. 

I analyze systems for a living, doctor. I've been a management analyst for over thirty years. If you want to hide a structural deficit in a company, you bury it in paperwork. That's what I always told my junior analysts. People just don't read the footnotes. I had this one kid working for me in '98, bright kid from Northwestern, but he completely missed a glaring discrepancy in a vendor contract because he just took the summary page at face value. You can't do that. You have to look at the raw data. And the data at my building shows exactly what they're doing.
Have you ever heard noises or voices that others around you don’t seem to hear?

No, no, I don't hear voices. I mean, I hear the noises in the walls, like I said, but that's just the physical reality of the building. The acoustics in those pre-war structures are fascinating, actually. They used lath and plaster back then, which has entirely different sound transmission properties than modern drywall. My grandfather was a carpenter—he used to build these beautiful, solid oak cabinets. You couldn't hear a thing through them. He'd spend weeks just sanding the edges perfectly smooth. He always said, "Measure twice, cut once." It's a shame nobody builds things to last anymore. Everything is just cheap materials and quick turnarounds. But no, to answer your question, I don't hear anything that isn't actually there. Just the deliberate banging they do to keep me on edge.
Do you believe that certain people or groups are specifically targeting you or trying to harm you personally, beyond what you’ve described with the property manager and neighbors?

No, no, nothing like that. It's really just confined to the property manager and the people in my building. I don't have some grand conspiracy with the government or the police after me or anything. 

Though, dealing with the local government reminds me of a consulting job I did for the municipal precinct back in... oh, it must have been 2004. They brought me in to streamline their dispatch protocols. The inefficiency was just staggering, doctor. They were still using this antiquated radio system that had dead zones all over the west side of the city. I remember driving through the west side to map out all the signal drops for my report, and I stopped at this little diner on 4th Avenue. Best cherry pie I've ever had in my life. The crust was perfectly flaky. You could tell it was made with real butter, not that cheap shortening they use in everything nowadays. 

My mother used to bake with real butter. She’d spend all Sunday morning in the kitchen, just covered in flour. We’d have roast beef, mashed potatoes, and a fresh pie every single week without fail. You just don't see families sitting down for a proper Sunday dinner anymore, do you? Everyone is just rushing around, eating fast food in their cars, staring at their phones. It completely ruins your digestion, eating like that. I read an article recently about how eating in a rushed state increases cortisol levels, which of course impacts your metabolic rate. But I suppose people just don't care about the long-term data.
Have you ever had any unusual thoughts or beliefs that other people might find strange or hard to understand, even outside of the issues you've been having at your apartment?

Strange? No, not at all. I'm a very grounded person, doctor. I deal in facts, in tangible metrics. I don't have time for unusual beliefs or superstitions. It's actually funny you ask that, because I've always been the one pointing out how irrational other people are. 

I remember back in '87, I had an administrative assistant—Susan. Lovely woman, very organized, but she was absolutely obsessed with astrology. She wouldn't schedule any of my important client meetings if Mercury was in retrograde. Can you imagine? Trying to explain to a corporate vice president that we have to push the quarterly risk assessment because of planetary alignment? She had this whole calendar on her desk covered in crystals and little moon stickers. Her desk was always a bit cluttered, actually. She had all these spider plants hanging everywhere. 

They're very resilient plants, spider plants. You can practically ignore them and they just keep growing and producing those little offshoots. My ex-wife tried to keep orchids once. Now, orchids, those require real precision. You have to get the humidity just right, the temperature... we had this little greenhouse window installed in our kitchen in the suburbs just for them. Cost a small fortune. The contractor who put it in did a terrible job with the sealant, though. The first heavy rain we had that April, water just poured right over the sill and ruined the hardwood floors. Real mahogany, too. It took three weeks to get the wood properly dried and refinished. The smell of that polyurethane sealant... it gives you a terrible headache if you don't ventilate the room properly. 

But no, I don't have any strange beliefs or anything like that. I just follow the data, and the data at my apartment is completely straightforward.
